back: Plan Schedule Management; Develop Schedule; Monitor and Control Schedule.

front: The four steps of Develop Schedule
back: 1. Define activities. 2. Determine sequence. 3. Estimate effort and duration. 4. Adjust.
Describes HOW the schedule will be developed, managed and controlled: units of measure, level of accuracy, control thresholds, reporting formats. Contains no dates.
The schedule model holds the activities, logic, durations and resources. The project schedule is an output of the model, showing planned dates, durations, milestones and resources.
The approved version of the schedule model. Changed only through formal change control; used for comparison with actual results.
All schedule activities, each with an identifier and a description of the work clear enough for the team to understand.
Extra detail for each activity: predecessors, successors, logical relationships, leads and lags, resource requirements, constraints and assumptions.
A significant point or event in a project. It has zero duration. May be mandatory (such as required by contract) or optional.
Work package: a deliverable, the lowest level of the WBS. Activity: the work needed to produce it, created by decomposing work packages.
A technique that shows activities as nodes linked by logical relationships to show the sequence of work.
The successor cannot start until the predecessor has finished. The most commonly used relationship.
The successor cannot finish until the predecessor has finished. Example: editing cannot finish until writing has finished.
The successor cannot start until the predecessor has started. Example: leveling concrete cannot start until pouring has started.
The successor cannot finish until the predecessor has started. Very rarely used.
Required by law, by contract or by the nature of the work. Also called hard logic.
A sequence chosen because it is good practice, although another order would work. Also called soft, preferred or preferential logic.
External: depends on something outside the project, such as a permit or supplier. Internal: between project activities, within the team's control.
The amount of time a successor activity can be advanced with respect to its predecessor. Often shown as a negative lag.
The amount of time a successor activity is delayed with respect to its predecessor. Example: waiting for concrete to cure.
Effort: the number of labor units required (such as 80 person-hours). Duration: the number of work periods needed with the estimated resources (such as 5 working days).
Uses actual data from a similar past project. Quick and cheap, less accurate. Used early, when little detail is known. Also called top-down.
Uses an algorithm or rate from historical data: quantity of work × time per unit.
Estimates the lower-level components and adds them up. Most accurate, most time-consuming.
Uses optimistic, most likely and pessimistic estimates to handle uncertainty in an estimate.
(O + M + P) ÷ 3. A simple average.
(O + 4M + P) ÷ 6. A weighted average that counts the most likely estimate four times.
The supporting documentation for an estimate: how it was developed, the assumptions, constraints and range.
Adding more of one resource while everything else stays fixed eventually gives smaller and smaller increases in output.
Near-term work is planned in detail; future work is planned at a higher level and detailed later.
Monitors project status to update the schedule and manages changes to the schedule baseline. Outputs: work performance information, schedule forecasts, change requests.
A prediction of the project's future timeline based on current progress and performance trends.
In adaptive projects, the rate at which deliverables are produced, validated and accepted per iteration.

front: Bar chart (Gantt chart) vs milestone chart
back: Bar chart: activities as bars over time, for tracking progress. Milestone chart: only key events, for reporting to management.
Estimating items by comparing them with each other instead of in hours or money. Fast; trades accuracy for speed. Examples: story points, T-shirt sizing, planning poker, affinity grouping.
Each team member privately picks a card with a point value; all cards are revealed at the same time; differences are discussed and the team re-estimates.
A bias in which the first number mentioned pulls later estimates toward it.
Quietly adding extra time to each estimate. The hidden buffers add up to an oversized schedule. Use a visible reserve instead.
Estimates have a wide range early in a project and the range narrows as more information becomes available.
